name: psql

flags.description: Specify database name to connect to
Execute a single command and exit
Stop a script at the first error

examples.description: Connect to specific database on localhost
Run a script safely, stopping on the first error

notes: Use \q to quit psql
Use \? for help on psql commands
Use ~/.pgpass or the PGPASSWORD env var rather than typing passwords in commands

name: pg_isready
description: Check whether a PostgreSQL server is accepting connections

flags.description: Quiet: only set the exit code

examples.command: until pg_isready -h db -q; do sleep 1; done
examples.description: Wait for a database in a startup script or CI

notes: Exit codes: 0 accepting, 1 rejecting (e.g. starting up), 2 no response, 3 no attempt made (bad parameters)
Doesn't check credentials; it only tests that the server accepts connections

name: createdb

flags.description: Specify the owner of the new database

notes: Requires appropriate PostgreSQL privileges

name: dropdb

flags.description: Don't error if database doesn't exist

notes: Cannot drop a database you are connected to
This action is irreversible
WARNING: permanently deletes the database and all its data; take a pg_dump first
Use --force (PostgreSQL 13+) to terminate existing connections

name: uuidv7()
description: Generate time-ordered UUIDs for primary keys (PostgreSQL 18+)

examples.command: CREATE TABLE orders (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(), total numeric);
examples.description: Use a time-ordered UUID as the default primary key
Read the creation timestamp embedded in v7 UUIDs
Random version 4 UUID (uuidv4() is an alias in 18+)

notes: v7 UUIDs sort roughly by creation time, so B-tree inserts stay local and indexes bloat less than with random v4 UUIDs
The timestamp is visible in the value; use v4 if IDs must not reveal creation time

name: GENERATED ALWAYS AS
description: Define computed columns: virtual (default in PostgreSQL 18+) or stored

examples.command: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN price_with_tax numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS (price * 1.2) VIRTUAL;
examples.description: Computed on read, uses no storage (PostgreSQL 18+)

examples.command: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN email_lower text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (lower(email)) STORED;
examples.description: Computed on write and stored like a normal column

examples.command: CREATE TABLE people (height_cm numeric, height_in numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS (height_cm / 2.54));
examples.description: No keyword: VIRTUAL on 18+, an error on older versions (which only support STORED)

notes: Expressions may only use immutable functions and the current row; no subqueries or other generated columns
Virtual columns can only use built-in functions and types; use STORED for user-defined functions or when you need to index the column

name: pg_dump

flags.description: Dump only schema: no data or statistics
Dump only data: no schema or statistics
Include/exclude objects listed in a file (PostgreSQL 17+)
Compression method/level, e.g. -Z zstd or -Z gzip:9 (custom/directory formats default to gzip)
Also dump optimizer statistics (PostgreSQL 18+; off by default)

examples.description: Recommended: compressed custom-format backup for pg_restore
Parallel directory dump compressed with zstd
Include planner statistics so the restored copy needs no immediate ANALYZE (PostgreSQL 18+)

notes: Custom format (-Fc) allows selective restore
Use pg_dumpall to backup all databases
Plain SQL dumps (the default) are restored with psql, not pg_restore
Use the pg_dump from the newest PostgreSQL version involved; it can dump older servers but not newer ones
pg_dump doesn't include roles; dump them separately with pg_dumpall --globals-only
Statistics are not included by default; without --statistics, run ANALYZE (or vacuumdb --analyze-only) after restoring

name: pg_restore
description: Restore a PostgreSQL database from archive

flags.description: List the archive's table of contents

examples.description: Fast parallel restore into another environment

notes: Only works with non-plain-text dumps
For plain SQL, use psql -f instead
-j works with custom (-Fc) and directory (-Fd) archives
WARNING: -c drops existing objects in the target database before recreating them

name: pg_dumpall
notes: Output is always plain SQL format; restore it with psql -f
Includes all databases, roles, and tablespaces

name: pg_basebackup
description: Take a physical base backup of a whole cluster (for replicas or PITR)

flags.description: Incremental backup against a previous backup's manifest (PostgreSQL 17+)

examples.description: Compressed tar backup of the local cluster

notes: Copies the entire cluster (all databases); for single databases use pg_dump
Restore incremental backups by merging them with pg_combinebackup (PostgreSQL 17+)

name: createuser

examples.description: Create user who can create databases

notes: Equivalent to CREATE ROLE with LOGIN
Passwords are hashed with SCRAM-SHA-256 by default; MD5 passwords are deprecated as of PostgreSQL 18

name: dropuser

flags.description: Don't error if user doesn't exist

notes: Cannot drop a user that owns objects

examples.description: List databases with size and description

notes: Run within psql interactive terminal

name: \c
description: Connect to a database in psql
notes: Switches current database connection

name: \dt
notes: Use \d tablename to describe a specific table

name: \d

examples.description: Show detailed table info including storage

notes: \d without argument lists all relations

name: \du
notes: Shows role attributes like superuser, createdb

name: \i
description: Execute SQL from file in psql

examples.description: Run file relative to current script

notes: \ir is useful for including files within scripts

name: \timing

examples.command: psql -c '\timing on' -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM orders;' mydb
examples.description: Time a single query from the shell

notes: Useful for performance analysis
Add \timing on to ~/.psqlrc to enable it always
Measures round-trip time as seen by the client; use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for server-side execution time

name: \x
notes: Displays rows vertically for better readability

name: \dn
description: List schemas in the current database

examples.description: List schemas with owners and privileges
List tables in a specific schema

name: \di

examples.description: List indexes in the search path
Indexes matching a pattern, with sizes

notes: \d tablename also shows a table's indexes

name: \copy
description: Import or export CSV data between a client-side file and a table

examples.description: Export a table to a local CSV

examples.command: \copy (SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE active) TO 'active.csv' CSV HEADER

examples.description: Import a local CSV into specific columns

notes: \copy reads/writes files on the client machine; SQL COPY uses the server's filesystem and needs extra privileges
Must be written on a single line

name: \conninfo
description: Show details about the current psql connection

examples.description: Show database, user, host, port, SSL and server details

notes: PostgreSQL 18's psql prints a table that also includes protocol version, SSL/GSSAPI details and whether you're a superuser; older versions print a single sentence
Client User shows who connected; Superuser reflects the current role, which can differ after SET ROLE

name: \watch
description: Re-run the current query repeatedly at an interval

examples.command: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active' \watch 5
examples.description: Re-run the query every 5 seconds until Ctrl+C

examples.command: SELECT now(), count(*) FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' \watch i=2 c=10
SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'running' \watch m=1
examples.description: Stop as soon as the query returns fewer than 1 row

notes: Default interval is 2 seconds; with an empty query buffer it re-runs the last query
The i= and c= options need psql 16+; m= needs psql 17+

name: \dx

examples.description: List every object that belongs to an extension

examples.command: SELECT name, default_version, installed_version FROM pg_available_extensions ORDER BY name;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;
examples.description: Install an extension in the current database

notes: Append x (e.g. \dxx) for expanded output in PostgreSQL 18+ psql; this works for most list commands
Extensions are per database: install them in each database that needs them

name: \startpipeline
description: Send several queries without waiting for each result (psql pipeline mode, PostgreSQL 18+)

examples.description: Send two inserts in one round trip and read all results at the end
Queue a parameterized query, then fetch results mid-pipeline
Show the pipeline status (off/on/abort) in the prompt

notes: \syncpipeline sends a sync point without ending the pipeline; \getresults [n] reads pending results
\g, \gx and COPY can't be used inside a pipeline
Mainly useful for testing pipelined workloads and reducing round trips over high-latency links

name: vacuumdb

flags.description: Only update optimizer statistics, don't vacuum
Analyze in 3 progressively thorough stages to get usable stats fast
Only analyze relations missing statistics (PostgreSQL 18+; with --analyze-only or --analyze-in-stages)

examples.description: Full vacuum for maximum space recovery
After pg_upgrade: quickly generate any statistics that weren't carried over (PostgreSQL 18+)
Refresh statistics on every database without vacuuming

notes: Regular vacuum is non-blocking
Full vacuum requires exclusive lock
WARNING: -f (VACUUM FULL) rewrites tables under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, blocking reads and writes
Autovacuum normally handles routine vacuuming; run vacuumdb --analyze-only after big imports or restores

name: reindexdb
notes: Useful after bulk operations
Can improve query performance

name: pg_upgrade
description: Upgrade a cluster to a new PostgreSQL major version in place, without dump and restore

flags.description: New version's bin directory (defaults to pg_upgrade's own)
Only check compatibility; don't change any data
Hard-link files instead of copying (fast; old cluster unusable once the new one starts)
Clone files with reflinks (fast, old cluster stays intact; needs Btrfs/XFS/APFS)
Move the old data directories into the new cluster (PostgreSQL 18+; potentially fastest, destroys the old cluster)

examples.description: Dry-run compatibility check before upgrading 17 to 18
Upgrade using hard links and 4 parallel jobs
Afterwards, generate any statistics that weren't carried over

notes: Both clusters must be stopped; initdb the new cluster first with matching locale/encoding settings
Run as the postgres OS user; add the same mode flag (e.g. --link) to --check so mode-specific checks run
PostgreSQL 18+ preserves most optimizer statistics (not extended statistics); older versions need a full vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages afterwards
WARNING: with --link or --swap the old cluster can't be safely used after the upgrade; take a backup first
Debian/Ubuntu packages wrap this as pg_upgradecluster

name: pg_ctl
notes: Requires appropriate permissions
Use -m immediate only as last resort
On packaged installs, use the service manager instead, e.g. sudo systemctl restart postgresql or brew services restart postgresql@18

name: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
description: Run a query and show its actual execution plan, row counts and timings

flags.description: Show shared buffer hits/reads (automatically included with ANALYZE in PostgreSQL 18+)
Show output columns and more detail
Show planner-related settings changed from their defaults
Also measure the cost of converting result rows for the client (PostgreSQL 17+, needs ANALYZE)
Plan a query containing $1, $2 placeholders without running it (PostgreSQL 16+)

examples.command: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
examples.description: Show the real plan and timing (includes buffer usage on PostgreSQL 18+)

examples.command: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day';
examples.description: Include buffer usage on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier

examples.command: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
examples.description: Estimated plan only, without running the query

examples.command: EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1;
examples.description: Plan a parameterized query copied from application logs

examples.command: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
examples.description: JSON plan to paste into a visualizer

examples.command: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now(); ROLLBACK;
examples.description: Analyze a write query without keeping its changes

notes: WARNING: ANALYZE actually executes the statement; wrap INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in a transaction and roll back
Compare estimated vs actual rows to spot stale statistics
PostgreSQL 18+ adds BUFFERS output automatically with ANALYZE; use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF) to hide it

name: VACUUM ANALYZE
description: Reclaim dead-row space and refresh planner statistics from SQL

examples.description: Refresh statistics for the whole database (fast, no vacuum)

examples.command: SELECT relname, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY relname;

notes: Plain VACUUM doesn't block reads or writes; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table under an exclusive lock
Can't run inside a transaction block

name: pg_stat_activity
description: Show current connections and running queries, and cancel or terminate them

examples.command: SELECT pid, usename, state, now() - query_start AS runtime, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle' ORDER BY runtime DESC;

examples.description: Cancel a running query by pid

notes: WARNING: pg_terminate_backend kills the session and rolls back its open transaction; try pg_cancel_backend first
